source.title: A survey of open questions in adaptive therapy: bridging mathematics and clinical translation

accepted.question_text: For adaptive cancer therapy, understood as dynamic patient-specific dose modulation or dose timing that maintains treatment-sensitive tumor cells so they competitively suppress treatment-resistant tumor cells, what cancer and model conditions are necessary for adaptive therapy to delay treatment resistance? In particular, when resistance is costly, resistant cells can be suppressed by competition with sensitive cells, and therapy reduces sensitive cells, what objectives should define therapeutic success, and do conclusions from simple sensitive/resistant-cell models remain valid when real-tumor components such as healthy cells, immune cells, resources, Allee effects, and phenotypic plasticity are included?
accepted.context_brief: Necessary model conditions for delaying resistance

evidence.quote: 1.1 What are the necessary conditions for adaptive therapy to delay resistance?

It is thought that the success of adaptive therapy in delaying the emergence of resistance depends on three characteristics of the cancer: a) resistance is costly, b) resistant cells can be suppressed by competition with sensitive cells, and c) therapy reduces the population of sensitive cells.

These simple models raise two further questions: 1) what are the appropriate objectives for evaluating the success of therapy? 2) do the main results hold up in models that include additional components of real tumors?

With the exception of the success of high dose therapy with a strong Allee effect, no universal therapy can achieve all three objectives of lowering average dose, delaying time to emergence of resistant cells, and reducing total tumor burden.

accepted.question_text: In adaptive cancer therapy models that rely on competition between treatment-sensitive and treatment-resistant cancer cells, how competitive are treatment-resistant phenotypes in actual tumors? Specifically, what is the biological nature of this competition, are resistant cells less competitive or do they pay a fitness cost without treatment, how do spatial arrangement, interaction ranges, shared resources, tumor architecture, and microenvironment alter competition, and are mutualism, commensalism, parasitism, or other ecological interactions important enough that simple frequency-dependent or density-dependent models are inadequate?

evidence.quote: 1.2 How competitive are treatment resistant phenotypes?
Adaptive therapy aims to exploit competition between treatment-sensitive and resistant cells. Key questions remain largely unanswered. First, what is the nature of this competition?
Second, are resistant cells less competitive?
Lastly, is competition the only important ecological interaction?
These observations suggest that our theoretical models of clonal dynamics during cancer treatment may be overly simplistic, and they underscore the need for more and better data.

accepted.question_text: What role should phenotypic plasticity and drug-induced mutations play in adaptive cancer therapy? Since treatment can induce or select resistant cellular states, phenotype switching between drug-sensitive and drug-resistant states can be reversible, and treatment holidays may re-sensitize resistant populations, when and how should adaptive therapy protocols account for switching rates, treatment-induced resistance, cancer-type and patient-level variability in plasticity, and the need to identify plasticity in an individual tumor before deciding whether and how to use adaptive therapy?

evidence.quote: 1.3 What is the role of plasticity and drug-induced mutations in adaptive therapy?
The effectiveness of treatment holidays drastically changes when considering phenotype switching between drug-sensitive and -resistant phenotypes.
Since phenotype switching to resistant states is often reversible (reviewed in [42]), treatment holidays have the potential to re-sensitize the resistant cell population to future drug rechallenges.
The switching rate from resistant to sensitive states can impact the benefit of adaptive therapy.
Thus, identifying the presence of phenotypic plasticity in a specific tumor could be an important factor in deciding if and how adaptive therapy should be applied.

accepted.question_text: How should adaptive cancer therapy models incorporate tissue homeostasis, normal cells, stromal cells, vasculature, immune cells, extracellular matrices, and environmentally mediated drug resistance when designing protocols to control cancer? Because cancer cells live in tissue ecosystems and may use stromal refuges that allow sensitive or resistant cells to survive therapy, should models evaluate how to manage or exploit environmentally mediated drug resistance, recapitulate the homeostasis disrupted by carcinogenesis, and design therapy-induced homeostasis rather than modeling only sensitive and resistant cancer cell populations?

evidence.quote: 1.4 What is the role of homeostasis and normal tissue in adaptive therapy?

In reality, the fitness of a cancer cell is not simply a cell-intrinsic property but includes its ability to take advantage of its dynamic tumor environment that includes not just other cancer cells but normal cells, vasculature, immune cells and extra-cellular matrices (see figure 2).

This environmentally mediated drug resistance (EMDR) explains why anti-cancer treatments prove less effective than otherwise expected. In the context of adaptive therapy, EMDR may provide the cancer cells with a therapy refuge regardless of whether they are resistant or sensitive to treatment.

Future adaptive therapy models should allow for EMDR. Such models could more faithfully incorporate the tumor microenvironment and the role of normal cells. Such models could then evaluate how best to manage or exploit EMDR when designing adaptive therapy protocols [55].
Hence, in improving the original adaptive therapy algorithm, we should consider the homeostasis that was disrupted by the tumor as well as the homeostasis that might be engineered by therapy.

accepted.question_text: For a cancer patient who may be eligible for either aggressive continuous therapy aimed at cure or adaptive therapy aimed at long-term containment, how should clinicians and modelers decide between treat-to-cure and treat-to-contain strategies before treatment begins? What disease characteristics, eco-evolutionary factors, biomarkers, resistant-cell frequencies, competition and tradeoffs, tumor burden, toxicity, quality of life, and practical monitoring constraints are needed to stratify patients into a continuous-therapy cohort versus an adaptive-therapy cohort, especially because a failed curative attempt can leave too many resistant cancer cells for later adaptive control?

evidence.quote: 2.1 Cure or control?
An explicit goal of adaptive therapy is to turn cancer into a chronic disease with sporadic (but life-long) management. Taking this approach likely means abandoning the hope of cure.
But is identifying such patients prior to treatment even possible?

So how does one decide between these opposing strategies? What key disease characteristics are needed to stratify patients into a treat-to-cure cohort (using continuous therapies) versus a treat-to-contain cohort (using adaptive therapies) [58]?
Cure or control could be favored depdending on the patient, the disease state, and the drugs used.

accepted.question_text: What adaptive dose administration protocol best balances tumor control, resistance delay, toxicity, clinical feasibility, and empirical robustness? In adaptive cancer therapy, should dosing use dose skipping or dose modulation; should tumor size be held near a maximal acceptable threshold to maximize competitive suppression; when should treatment switch to maximum tolerated dose if resistant cells are partially resistant; how should stabilization doses and dose titration be chosen; and how should protocols respond to tumor size changes, spatial structure, cell mobility, quiescence, and other phenomena that simple models may miss?

evidence.quote: 2.2 What is the optimal adaptive dose administration protocol?

Many models emphasize competition between sensitive and highly resistant cells and assume that the larger the tumor size, the stronger the competition [70, 57, 2, 67, 71, 72, 32, 25]. Such models suggest maintaining the tumor at the maximal acceptable size, in order to maximize competitive suppression of resistance [63, 25].

The switching time could be timed with a decrease of treatment efficiency [73], but the practical implementation and whether similar conclusions hold for models with many types of tumor cells [76] remains to be investigated.
A practical question is to determine the appropriate stabilization dose.
This highlights that simple models may miss important phenomena and that more data and modeling are needed to optimize adaptive therapies.

accepted.question_text: How can mathematical modeling support wet-lab testing of adaptive cancer therapy so that experiments validate theory, assess safety, and guide protocol design for patients? In particular, how should experiments be designed to measure competitive suppression in a cancer; how should drug resistance be represented by mixing pre-evolved resistant and sensitive cells, allowing resistance to evolve during the experiment, using clone tracking, or another approach; and how should treatment algorithms from mathematical or experimental models be translated to clinical practice despite pharmacokinetics, differing animal and patient time scales, toxicity, machine failures, weekends or holidays, and other deviations from planned schedules?
accepted.context_brief: Using models to design wet-lab tests

evidence.quote: 2.3 How can we leverage mathematical modelling to support testing of adaptive therapy in the wet lab?
To do so requires experimental platforms for testing and, if necessary, improving the safety and efficacy of adaptive protocols.
Surveying the experimental literature on adaptive therapy, and based on our own experience, we identify three areas in need of further research.
First, how do we design experiments to assess the competitive suppression in a particular cancer and thus the scope for such patients to benefit from adaptive therapy?
Second, there is the question of how drug-resistance is modeled in the wet lab.
Finally, there is the question of how to translate treatment algorithms from mathematical or experimental models into clinical practice.
This raises the question of how robust are adaptive schedules to deviations, and what is the best strategy with which to respond when deviations occur.

accepted.question_text: What best practices should guide adaptive therapy algorithms when multiple drugs are available? Since the number of possible treatment combinations expands rapidly, how should models and trials reduce combinatorial complexity while choosing drug combinations, timing, and ordering; when should strategies such as evolutionary cycling, double-bind therapy, primary-secondary adaptive therapy, or extinction therapy be used; and what clinical evidence is needed for these multi-drug adaptive approaches?

evidence.quote: 2.4 What are best practices to design adaptive algorithms for multiple drugs?
It remains unclear how to extend adaptive therapy approaches to multiple treatments. When multiple drugs are available, the combinatorial possibilities expand rapidly.
This study and others [73, 95, 94, 96] illustrate the feasibility of model-driven treatment planning to reduce the combinatorial complexity for multi-drug adaptive therapies.
An alternative multidrug adaptive approach is to identify collaterally sensitive treatments such that resistance to first line treatment induces sensitivity to secondary treatments [33, 97].

While models of extinction therapy have been developed [102], clinical evidence is sparse but supported by the standard of care multi-step curative treatment in Pediatric Acute Lymphocytic Leukemia [107], by two case studies involving cure in patients with metastatic breast cancer [108, 109], and an ongoing clinical trial for patients with pediatric rhabdomyosarcoma [110].

accepted.question_text: Is real-time patient-specific prediction feasible for adaptive therapy, and what monitoring, model calibration, validation, sensitivity analysis, identifiability analysis, and biomarker quality are required before predictions should guide dose modulation? Given a clinical marker such as prostate-specific antigen, circulating tumor DNA, circulating tumor cells, urine markers, imaging, or another disease-specific biomarker, when can a mathematical model accurately describe patient-specific dynamics well enough to predict subsequent response, and when should it be rejected because it cannot describe the data?

evidence.quote: 3.1 Is real-time patient prediction feasible?
Predicting precisely when a patient will progress during adaptive therapy offers the opportunity to appropriately modulate treatment, thereby extending patient response and survival.
This requires sufficient monitoring of an individual patient’s disease using appropriate clinical markers.
Prior to making model predictions, the chosen model should be calibrated and validated to demonstrate that it can accurately describe patient-specific biomarker dynamics [111].
If the model cannot accurately describe the data, then it should not be used to make predictions of subsequent patient responses.
Model-predictions are dependent on the quality and time-resolution of patient-specific biomarkers.

accepted.question_text: Do the adverse effects and risks of maintaining a relatively high tumor burden in adaptive therapy outweigh the benefits of stronger competitive suppression of resistant cells? For containment strategies that delay resuming therapy until sensitive cells create strong frequency-dependent and density-dependent suppression of resistant cells, how should models and trials balance prolonged treatment sensitivity against symptoms, biomarker accuracy and measurement frequency, additional cancer evolution under on/off therapy, new metastases, lesion-level heterogeneity across metastatic sites, quality-of-life costs, and disease-specific or drug-specific safety limits?
accepted.context_brief: Risks of maintaining high tumor burden

evidence.quote: 3.2 Do adverse effects of maintaining high tumor burden negate potential benefit?

The prostate adaptive trial does provide some evidence that prolonged sensitivity may outweigh adverse effects of maintaining high tumor burden, but the promise of being able to perpetually control each patient’s disease did not happen. Why not?

Yet, there are likely dangers associated with containment strategies aiming for overall high, and persistent tumor burdens. These fall into four important categories: 1) patients becoming symptomatic, 2) the ability of the biomarker to be sufficiently accurate and measurable frequently, 3) subsequent cancer evolution during the period of adaptive therapy, and 4) risk of new metastases.

As more clinical trials of adaptive therapy emerge from integrating mathematical models with clinical opportunity and need, it will be essential to consider the trade-offs associated with maintaining relatively large tumor burdens.

Balancing these costs and benefits will likely be disease and drug specific, and will require a continued lockstep between mathematical models and empirical studies, data and observations of patients.

accepted.question_text: Can mathematical models reliably drive individual cancer treatment decisions in adaptive or evolution-based therapy? What must change in patient-data collection, prediction under uncertainty, interdisciplinary communication, and decision-support workflows so that predictive mathematical models can track patient-specific tumor dynamics, compare available treatment options using mechanisms such as virtual-patient cohorts in a Phase i framework, and provide clinically useful recommendations at scale?

evidence.quote: 3.3 Can a mathematical model drive treatment decision making?
Therefore, there is a great need for clinically suitable predictive mathematical models that track patient-specific tumor dynamics.
There are, however, numerous challenges that need to be surmounted for this approach to be broadly successful and able to be scaled to large numbers of patients.

To move into predictive mathematical modeling, we must rethink how we collect patient data, in that we don’t want to simply detect progression, but rather quantify and understand the tumor dynamics prior to progression such that one can inform treatment decisions to avoid it.
Even an optimally designed data collection protocol that would optimize model predictability will still leave significant uncertainties in such predictions.
The basic principle is to develop cohorts of virtual patients derived from a calibrated mathematical model, and apply “clinical trials” to such cohorts with varying regimens of treatment.

Perhaps the most important challenge concerns the communication between different disciplines: the practice of oncology, the theories of ecology and evolution, and the application of mathematical models to data were not historically in sync in terms of possibilities for both practice and outcome.
